vsm1.2:56.1: ix. The tree-root-dweller’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse a roof”
vsm1.2:56.3: The tree-root dweller should avoid such trees as a tree near a frontier, a shrine tree, a gum tree, a fruit tree,
vsm1.2:56.4:
a bats’ tree, a hollow tree, or a tree standing in the middle of a monastery. He can choose
a tree standing on the outskirts of a monastery. These are the directions.
vsm1.2:57.2: Herein, one who is strict is not allowed to have a tree that he has chosen tidied up.
vsm1.2:57.3: He can move the fallen leaves with his foot while dwelling there.
vsm1.2:57.4: The medium one is allowed to get it tidied up by those who happen to come along.
vsm1.2:57.5:
The mild one can take up residence there after summoning monastery attendants and novices and getting
them to clear it up, level it, strew sand and make a fence round with a gate fixed in it.
vsm1.2:57.6: On a special day, a tree-root dweller should sit in some concealed place elsewhere rather than there.
vsm1.2:57.7: The moment any one of these three makes his abode under a roof, his ascetic practice is broken.
vsm1.2:57.8:
The reciters of the Aṅguttara say that it is broken as soon as he knowingly meets
the dawn under a roof. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:58.2:
perception of impermanence is aroused through seeing the continual alteration of young leaves;
avarice about abodes and love of building work are absent;
vsm1.2:58.3: he dwells in the company of deities; he lives in conformity with the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:59.1:
The Blessed One praised roots of trees
As one of the dependencies (Vin I 58);
Can he that loves secludedness
Find such another dwelling place?
vsm1.2:59.2:
Secluded at the roots of trees
And guarded well by deities
He lives in true devotedness
Nor covets any dwelling place.
vsm1.2:59.3:
And when the tender leaves are seen
Bright red at first, then turning green,
And then to yellow as they fall,
He sheds belief once and for all
vsm1.2:59.4:
In permanence. Tree roots have been
Bequeathed by him; secluded scene
No wise man will disdain at all
For contemplating rise and fall.
vsm1.2:59.5:
This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the tree-root-dweller’s practice.
vsm1.2:60.1: x. The open-air-dweller’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse a roof and a tree root”
vsm1.2:60.3: An open-air dweller is allowed to enter the Uposatha-house for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma or for the purpose of the Uposatha.
vsm1.2:60.4: If it rains while he is inside, he can go out when the rain is over instead of going out while it is still raining.
vsm1.2:60.5:
He is allowed to enter the eating hall or the fire room in order to do the duties, or to go
under a roof in order to ask elder bhikkhus in the eating hall about a meal,
vsm1.2:60.6: or when teaching and taking lessons, or to take beds, chairs, etc., inside that have been wrongly left outside.
vsm1.2:60.7: If he is going along a road with a requisite belonging to a senior and it rains, he is allowed to go into a wayside rest house.
vsm1.2:60.8: If he has nothing with him, he is not allowed to hurry in order to get to a rest house;
vsm1.2:60.9:
but he can go at his normal pace and enter it and stay there as long as it rains.
These are the directions for it. And the same rule applies to the tree-root dweller too.
vsm1.2:61.2: Herein, one who is strict is not allowed to live near a tree or a rock or a house.
vsm1.2:61.3: He should make a robe-tent right out in the open and live in that.
vsm1.2:61.4: The medium one is allowed to live near a tree or a rock or a house so long as he is not covered by them.
vsm1.2:61.5:
The mild one is allowed these: a rock overhang without a drip-ledge cut in it, a hut of branches,
cloth stiffened with paste, and a tent treated as a fixture, that has been left by field watchers, and so on.
vsm1.2:61.6: The moment any one of these three goes under a roof or to a tree root to dwell there, his ascetic practice is broken.
vsm1.2:61.7: The reciters of the Aṅguttara say that it is broken as soon as he knowingly meets the dawn there. This is the breach in this case.
vsm1.2:62.1: The benefits are these: the impediment of dwellings is severed; stiffness and torpor are expelled;
vsm1.2:62.2:
his conduct deserves the praise “Like deer the bhikkhus live unattached and homeless” (S I 199); he is detached;
he is free to go in any direction; he lives in conformity with the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:63.1:
The open air provides a life
That aids the homeless bhikkhu’s strife,
Easy to get, and leaves his mind
Alert as a deer, so he shall find
vsm1.2:63.2:
Stiffness and torpor brought to halt.
Under the star-bejewelled vault
The moon and sun furnish his light,
And concentration his delight.
vsm1.2:63.3:
The joy seclusion’s savour gives
He shall discover soon who lives
In open air; and that is why
The wise prefer the open sky.
vsm1.2:63.4: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the open-air-dweller’s practice.
vsm1.2:64.1:
xi. The charnel-ground-dweller’s practice is undertaken with one of the following
statements: “I refuse what is not a charnel ground”
vsm1.2:64.3:
Now, the charnel-ground dweller should not live in some place just because the people
who built the village have called it “the charnel ground”
vsm1.2:64.4: for it is not a charnel ground unless a dead body has been burnt on it.
vsm1.2:64.5:
But as soon as one has been burnt on it, it becomes a charnel ground. And even if
it has been neglected for a dozen years, it is so still.
vsm1.2:65.1:
One who dwells there should not be the sort of person who gets walks, pavilions, etc., built,
has beds and chairs set out and drinking and washing water kept ready, and preaches Dhamma;
vsm1.2:65.2:
for this ascetic practice is a momentous thing. Whoever goes to live there should be diligent. And he should first
inform the senior elder of the Order or the king’s local representative in order to prevent trouble.
vsm1.2:65.3: When he walks up and down, he should do so looking at the pyre with half an eye.
vsm1.2:65.4:
On his way to the charnel ground he should avoid the main roads and take a by-path.
He should define all the objects there while it is day,
vsm1.2:65.5:
so that they will not assume frightening shapes for him at night. Even if non-human beings
wander about screeching, he must not hit them with anything.
vsm1.2:65.6: It is not allowed to miss going to the charnel ground even for a single day.
vsm1.2:65.7:
The reciters of the Aṅguttara say that after spending the middle watch in the charnel
ground he is allowed to leave in the last watch.
vsm1.2:65.8:
He should not take such foods as sesame flour, pease pudding, fish, meat, milk,
oil, sugar, etc., which are liked by non-human beings.
vsm1.2:65.9: He should not enter the homes of families. These are the directions for it.
vsm1.2:66.2: Herein, one who is strict should live where there are always burnings and corpses and mourning.
vsm1.2:66.3:
The medium one is allowed to live where there is one of these three. The mild one is allowed to live in a place
that possesses the bare characteristics of a charnel ground already stated.
vsm1.2:66.4: When any one of these three makes his abode in some place not a charnel ground, his ascetic practice is broken.
vsm1.2:66.5: It is on the day on which he does not go to the charnel ground, the Aṅguttara reciters say. This is the breach in this case.
vsm1.2:67.1:
The benefits are these. He acquires mindfulness of death; he lives diligently;
the sign of foulness is available (see Ch. VI); greed for sense desires is removed;
vsm1.2:68.1:
Even in sleep the dweller in a charnel ground shows naught
Of negligence, for death is ever present to his thought;
He may be sure there is no lust after sense pleasure preys
Upon his mind, with many corpses present to his gaze.
vsm1.2:68.2:
Rightly he strives because he gains a sense of urgency,
While in his search for final peace he curbs all vanity.
Let him that feels a leaning to Nibbāna in his heart
Embrace this practice for it has rare virtues to impart.
vsm1.2:68.3:
This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades,
breach, and benefits, in the case of the charnel-ground dweller’s practice.
vsm1.2:69.1: xii. The any-bed-user’s practice is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I refuse greed for resting places”
vsm1.2:69.3: The any-bed user should be content with whatever resting place he gets thus: “This falls to your lot.”
vsm1.2:69.4: He must not make anyone else shift from his bed.
vsm1.2:70.2:
Herein, one who is strict is not allowed to ask about the resting place that has fallen to his lot: “Is it far?” or “Is it
too near?” or “Is it infested by non-human beings, snakes, and so on?” or “Is it hot?” or “Is it cold?”.
vsm1.2:70.3: The medium one is allowed to ask, but not to go and inspect it.
vsm1.2:70.4: The mild one is allowed to inspect it and, if he does not like it, to choose another.
vsm1.2:70.5:
As soon as greed for resting places arises in any one of these three, his ascetic
practice is broken. This is the breach in this instance.
vsm1.2:71.1:
The benefits are these. The advice “He should be content with what he gets” (J-a I 476;
Vin IV 259) is carried out; he regards the welfare of his fellows in the life of purity;
vsm1.2:71.2:
he gives up caring about inferiority and superiority; approval and disapproval are abandoned; the door is closed
against excessive wishes; he lives in conformity with the principles of fewness of wishes, and so on.
vsm1.2:72.1:
One vowed to any bed will be
Content with what he gets, and he
Can sleep in bliss without dismay
On nothing but a spread of hay.
vsm1.2:72.2:
He is not eager for the best,
No lowly couch does he detest,
He aids his young companions too
That to the monk’s good life are new.
vsm1.2:72.3:
So for a wise man to delight
In any kind of bed is right;
A Noble One this custom loves
As one the sages’ Lord approves.
vsm1.2:72.4: This is the commentary on the undertaking, directions, grades, breach, and benefits, in the case of the any-bed-user’s practice.
